subject: greenblatt

brief.inclusion: Chief executive and national director of the Anti-Defamation League since 2015, running a $135 million organization whose definitions of antisemitism, extremism research, law-enforcement partnerships and statements on campus protest, platforms and Israel shape policy debate in Washington and the states.
brief.namesakes: FEC records include several other Jonathan Greenblatts: a Washington lawyer (Shearman & Sterling, Legal Innovators, J Greenblatt International Disputes), a New Hampshire health-system employee, and a New York contributor filing as "not employed" (61 rows, including 2020–2024 gifts to Biden and Harris committees). Only rows naming Ethos Water, GOOD Worldwide, Starbucks, the White House or the ADL are counted.

coverage.lags: The latest ADL Form 990 on ProPublica covers the fiscal year ending June 2025.

openQuestions: The 61 New York "not employed" FEC rows may include Greenblatt; they are excluded until an address or employer confirms identity.
The March 2024 Morning Joe keffiyeh remark is quoted only in fragments; check the full MSNBC transcript.

summary: Former Clinton and Obama White House official and social entrepreneur (co-founder of Ethos Water) who has led the Anti-Defamation League since July 2015. He has made the ADL a combatant on several fronts: declaring in 2022 that anti-Zionism is antisemitism, clashing with and then defending Elon Musk, calling campus pro-Palestinian groups Iran's "campus proxies" in 2024, and in 2026 describing "the most concentrated, most dangerous surge of antisemitism in living memory." The ADL reported revenue of $135.3 million and paid him $1.13 million in fiscal 2025.

chapters.title: Democratic staffer and social entrepreneur
chapters.dek: Two White Houses, a bottled-water company and a career in "social innovation."
chapters.body:
Greenblatt was born on November 21, 1970, in Trumbull, Connecticut, to a Jewish family; his grandfather survived the Holocaust [[wikipedia]]. After graduating from Tufts in 1992 he worked on Bill Clinton's campaign, then in the Clinton White House and the Commerce Department on international economic policy. He later earned an MBA at Northwestern's Kellogg School [[wikipedia]].

In 2002 he co-founded Ethos Water with Peter Thum, a brand that funded clean-water projects; Starbucks bought it in 2005 for $8 million and made him a vice president [[wikipedia, fec-greenblatt]]. He went on to found the volunteer platform All for Good and to run GOOD Worldwide [[wikipedia]]. From 2011 to 2014 he was special assistant to President Obama and director of the White House Office of Social Innovation and Civic Participation [[wikipedia]].

chapters.title: Running the ADL
chapters.dek: A $135 million organization built on monitoring, education and law-enforcement partnerships.
chapters.body:
Greenblatt became chief executive and national director of the Anti-Defamation League on July 20, 2015, succeeding Abraham Foxman [[wikipedia]]. The organization has grown under him: in the fiscal year ending June 2025 it reported revenue of $135.3 million and paid him $1,127,131, plus $198,905 from related organizations [[propublica-adl]].

His annual State of Hate address sets out the ADL's agenda. In March 2026 he said Jews faced "the most concentrated, most dangerous surge of antisemitism in living memory," citing 20 Jews murdered in the past year, and described ADL work on more than 60 bills in over 30 states, more than 1,000 alerts to law enforcement, and advocacy that helped secure more than half a billion dollars in security funding for at-risk institutions [[adl-state-of-hate-2026]]. In 2025 Time named him one of its 100 most influential people [[wikipedia]].

chapters.title: Anti-Zionism, campuses and the war in Gaza
chapters.dek: A definitional line in 2022 and a fight with campus activists after October 7.
chapters.body:
At the ADL's leadership summit on May 1, 2022, Greenblatt said anti-Zionism is antisemitism, calling it an ideology "rooted in rage" and "predicated on one concept: the negation of another people" [[jta-antizionism-2022]]. The position drew criticism from the left and from some ADL staff [[wikipedia]].

After October 7, 2023, and the campus protests over the war in Gaza, his television appearances became flashpoints. In late March 2024 on MSNBC's Morning Joe he said that if people would not tolerate someone calling for death to Zionists while wearing a swastika, "you should not tolerate it if you're wearing a keffiyeh on their head." CAIR and about 60 allied groups called for his firing; he said his words had been taken out of context and "I'm not comparing the garb" [[algemeiner-keffiyeh-2024, cair-proxies-2024]]. In April, during the Columbia encampment protests, CAIR quoted him on the same program calling Students for Justice in Palestine and Jewish Voice for Peace Iran's "campus proxies," and asked MSNBC to stop booking him [[beast-proxies-2024, cair-proxies-2024]]. That year Wikipedia's editors downgraded the ADL's reliability on the Israeli–Palestinian conflict, citing his statements [[wikipedia]].

chapters.title: Musk and the platforms
chapters.dek: From adversary to defender and back.
chapters.body:
Platform policy is a core ADL issue, and Elon Musk's ownership of X made it personal. Greenblatt praised Musk in 2022 and later apologized for calling him "the Henry Ford of our time" [[wikipedia]]. In September 2023 Musk threatened to sue the ADL, blaming it for advertisers leaving X; the ADL called his attacks "dangerous and deeply irresponsible," and weeks later Greenblatt was again praising him as an "amazing entrepreneur and extraordinary innovator" [[aljazeera-musk-2025]].

On January 20, 2025, the ADL said Musk's raised-arm gesture at Trump's inauguration rally was "an awkward gesture in a moment of enthusiasm," not a Nazi salute. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and several Jewish groups rejected that reading. Three days later Greenblatt condemned Musk's Nazi-themed puns about the episode [[aljazeera-musk-2025, wikipedia]].
